newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian industry sees PM Gujral pushing reforms.
newsitem.headline: Indian industry sees PM Gujral pushing reforms.

text.p: India's economic reforms were safe with Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's centre-left alliance despite the loss of reform-minded former finance minister P. Chidambaram, industry leaders said on Monday.
Indications that Gujral will support Chidambaram's pathbreaking 1997/98 (April-March) budget, to be taken up by parliament later in April, heartened Indian industry.
"His (Gujral's) indication is he will go by the old budget," the speaker of the lower house, P.A. Sangma said, referring to Chidambaram's investor-friendly plan.
"The United Front cannot disown a budget by its own government," V. Raghuraman, secretary general of Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry (Assocham) told Reuters.
"It gives us confidence. But there are several challenges facing the government."
Gujral assumed power on Monday at the head of a cabinet nearly identical to that of his predecessor, H.D. Deve Gowda, who lost a vote of confidence on April 11.
Gujral said he would keep the post of foreign minister and would also take on the finance minister portfolio.

The benchmark Bombay 30-share stock index soared on Gujral's swearing-in, gaining 101.54 points or 2.75 percent to close at a provisional 3,798.06 on investor relief that India's three-week political crisis had ended.
Shares on the Bombay-based National Stock Exchange and on other regional bourses like Calcutta gained more than one percent.

The Indian rupee firmed as well, but dealers attributed that to inaction by the central bank to stop the rupee's rise rather than political developments. In late afternoon trade, the rupee was at 35.762 to the dollar after opening at 35.79/80.
But the absence of Chidambaram, whose regional party decided not to join the government, had raised questions about the future course of economic and budgetary policy.
Despite Chidambaram's absence, the government will likely toe his economic policies and woo foreign investors, business leaders said. But it faces some critical economic decisions.
India began opening up to trade and investment in 1991 under former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.
"The economic policy on which our budget has been based will remain more or less the same, maybe some minor changes here or there," Gujral later told reporters.
Chidambaram's absence from the cabinet will neither hinder the passage of the business-friendly budget, which was drafted by him, nor slow down economic reforms, businessmen said.

"Individuals have their place but the government is committed to liberalisation and the good of the common man," A.S. Kasliwal, president of Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), told Reuters.
Kasliwal said it was up to domestic industry to promote higher growth.
Gujral, after being sworn in by President Shankar Dayal Sharma in the ornate presidential palace, told reporters that his government will continue to strengthen economic reforms.

The United Front was committed to implementing its Common Minimum Programme (CMP), a policy blueprint unveiled by the alliance last year which sets a target of attracting $10 billion in foreign direct investment per year, Gujral said on Sunday.
The government must focus on infrastructure, which is crucial in achieving higher growth, Raghuraman said.
"We have to see how it tackles infrastructure. They have to take a decision on the rising deficit on the oil pool account," he said.

The oil pool deficit is the amount the government owes state-owned oil companies as subsidies for selling output well below international prices. The deficit was estimated at 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) at the beginning of the current fiscal year on April 1.
Analysts have said India will have to take the politically unpopular step of raising the prices of petroleum products to bridge the soaring oil subsidy bill. $1 = 35.8 rupees
